values.value: • Keep urgency alive by tying it to a dated plan and named owners. • Confirm the cost of delay in business, learner, institutional, or operational terms. • Translate urgency into agreed next steps and dates. • Use the senior executive concern to bring in the final approver faster. • Protect the timeline from drifting into endless discussion.
4|Yes & Urgent
Buyer may say, 'We know it is urgent, but the team is stretched.' Response: 'Then let us reduce the lift on your side and agree the minimum next steps needed to keep momentum.'
Urgency exists. Tie it to timeline, decision owner, and next meeting so urgency converts into action.
Low risk. Convert urgency into a close plan.
Ask: 'Since this is urgent, what decision needs to happen by when, and who signs it off?'
Yes & Urgent

• Turn acknowledged need into action by quantifying the downside of waiting. • Ask what changes if the issue is left untouched for one quarter or one semester. • Find a date-linked trigger such as admissions cycle, compliance deadline, hiring wave, or budget window. • Create a first phase that feels easy to start now. • Move the deal from agreement to commitment.
4|Yes but Not urgent
Buyer may say, 'This matters, but not immediately.' Response: 'Understood. What changes if this remains unresolved for one more quarter or term? That will help us set the right pace.'
Build urgency by quantifying the cost of delay. Link the issue to revenue, learner impact, compliance, or rollout risk.
Risk: The deal can drag without a deadline.
Ask: 'What happens if this slips by one quarter for the business or institution?'
Yes but Not urgent

• Do not lead with solution detail until the reason to buy is clear. • Ask what problem this is solving, for whom, and what happens if it is ignored. • Probe whether the issue is strategic, operational, or only exploratory. • Get one senior stakeholder to describe the cost of the current state. • Then frame your offer around that pain, not around features.
4|Unclear
Buyer may say, 'We are still exploring options.' Response: 'That is fine. Before options, I want to make sure we are solving the right problem and not just discussing features.'
Do not jump to solutioning. First make the pain specific, visible, and expensive enough to act on.
Risk: Weak pain means weak buying intent.
Ask: 'Which team, metric, or student outcome is suffering today because this is not solved?'
Unclear

• Step back and rediscover the case for change from scratch. • Find out who raised the issue, who feels the pain, and who benefits if solved. • Use plain business language, not product language, to surface the real need. • Do not chase proposal or demo until the buying reason is explicit. • This deal needs discovery, not persuasion.
4|Don't know
Buyer may say, 'Let us start with a presentation.' Response: 'Happy to, but it will be far more useful if I first understand what the real business or learner issue is.'
Find the real trigger before progressing. Without a clear reason to buy, every next step will feel polite but empty.
High risk: No clear buying reason.
Ask: 'Why is this important now, and what changes if nothing is done?'
Don't know
Are the Customer's reasons to buy tied to a specific, compelling need, which is acknowledged by the sr. executives
